cyber_essentials.title: Cyber Essentials
cyber_essentials.intro: Ten scenario questions covering the five Cyber Essentials technical controls — Firewalls, Secure Configuration, Security Update Management, User Access Control and Malware Protection. Sourced directly from NCSC's own “Cyber Essentials: Requirements for IT Infrastructure v3.3” (Crown Copyright).

learn.heading: Firewalls
learn.body:
A firewall is the security filter between your devices and the internet — it decides what traffic gets in and out, based on rules you or your IT provider set. Left on factory defaults, a firewall's own admin interface is often the weakest point in the whole setup: if an attacker can log into the firewall itself, every rule it enforces becomes irrelevant, since they can simply switch protection off or reconfigure it from the inside.

The core requirements: change every device's default admin password to something strong and unique, or disable remote admin access entirely if it isn't needed. Keep the admin interface off the internet unless there's a genuine business need — and if there is, protect it with MFA or a trusted IP allow list. Block unauthenticated inbound connections by default, so nothing gets in unless a documented, approved rule specifically lets it. And remove firewall rules once they're no longer needed, rather than letting them quietly accumulate over time. Any device that connects to networks you don't control — a laptop on public wifi, say — needs its own software firewall, since there's no boundary firewall protecting it out there.

learn.heading: Secure Configuration
learn.body:
Devices don't arrive secure by default. Out-of-the-box settings often include a known admin password, spare user accounts nobody asked for, and unnecessary software quietly running in the background — any of which gives an attacker somewhere to start. Secure Configuration is about proactively closing those gaps before they get found.

That means regularly removing or disabling accounts nobody's using (including default guest and admin accounts), changing any default or guessable passwords, removing software and services that aren't actually needed, and disabling auto-run features that let files execute without anyone approving them first. Devices also need a real credential — a password, PIN, or biometric — before anyone can use them, protected against someone simply guessing it over and over: throttling repeated attempts, or locking the device out after no more than 10 failed tries.

learn.heading: Security Update Management
learn.body:
Every piece of software eventually has security flaws discovered in it — vulnerabilities that attackers actively hunt for once they're public knowledge, because a patch announcement effectively tells everyone exactly where the weakness was. The requirement: keep all software licensed and supported, and apply updates fixing anything rated “critical” or “high risk” (a CVSS v3 score of 7 or higher) within 14 days of release, sooner where practical. Automatic updates should be switched on wherever that's an option.

Once a vendor stops supporting a product entirely, any new vulnerability discovered in it will simply never be fixed. That means unsupported software needs to come off any in-scope device — or be walled off from the internet entirely, in its own isolated sub-set — rather than staying connected and permanently exposed with no way to close the gap.

learn.heading: User Access Control
learn.body:
Every account is a door into your systems, and the level of access it carries determines how much damage gets done if the wrong person walks through it. Organisations need a real process for creating and approving accounts, unique credentials for every user, and accounts removed or disabled the moment they're no longer needed — when someone leaves, for instance, or after a defined period of inactivity.

Administrative accounts need particular care: they should be used only for admin tasks, never for everyday email or web browsing, because malware that reaches a device runs with whatever privileges the logged-in account already has. An admin account opening one malicious attachment can hand malware far more reach across a network than a standard account ever could. Multi-factor authentication should be used wherever it's available, and is mandatory for cloud services and anything reachable from the internet — a password alone, easily phished, guessed, or reused from an unrelated data breach somewhere else, isn't enough on its own to keep an internet-facing account safe.

learn.heading: Malware Protection
learn.body:
Malware — viruses, worms, ransomware and similar — usually arrives through malicious email attachments, downloads, or software installed without proper vetting. Left unchecked, it can corrupt systems, steal or destroy data, or spread quietly to other parts of a network before anyone notices anything's wrong.

Every in-scope device needs at least one of two protections. Anti-malware software: kept active, updated in line with the vendor's instructions, and configured to block malware execution, malicious code, and connections to known-bad websites. Or application allow listing: only pre-approved, code-signed applications are permitted to run at all, and everything else — old threats and brand-new ones alike — is blocked by default rather than by recognition. The two approaches work differently (one reacts to known threats, the other blocks anything unapproved regardless of whether it's ever been seen before), which is why either is acceptable — but neither is a case of “install once and forget.”

questions.scenario: Your IT contractor sets up remote access to your office firewall's admin interface so they can manage it from home — using the firewall's factory default admin password, since nobody's got round to changing it.
questions.question: Which Cyber Essentials requirement does this breach?
options: Nothing — factory passwords are fine as long as the interface isn't advertised publicly
Default admin passwords must be changed to a strong, unique password — or remote admin access disabled entirely
Firewalls only need protecting if the office uses public wifi
Only cloud firewalls require a password change
questions.explanation: For every firewall, you must change default administrative passwords to a strong and unique password — or disable remote administrative access entirely. Internet-facing admin interfaces additionally need MFA or an IP allow list.
questions.why: The admin interface is the master control for everything the firewall protects — if an attacker can log into it, every other firewall rule stops mattering, because they can simply reconfigure or switch off the protection itself. A factory default password is public information (it's in the manual), so leaving it unchanged is functionally the same as leaving the front door key under the mat with a sign pointing to it.
questions.reference: Cyber Essentials: Requirements for IT Infrastructure v3.3 — Section E.1, Firewalls

questions.scenario: A new starter's laptop is connected straight to the office network before IT has applied any configuration at all.
questions.question: What must the firewall do by default with any inbound connection that hasn't been explicitly allowed?
options: Allow it through, then log it for review later
Block unauthenticated inbound connections by default
Only block it if the source is outside the UK
Ask the user to confirm by email first
questions.explanation: Cyber Essentials requires that unauthenticated inbound connections are blocked by default — nothing gets in unless a documented, approved firewall rule lets it.
questions.why: Every internet-connected device is constantly scanned by automated tools looking for anything that responds — this starts within minutes of a device going online, not just when someone specifically targets your business. Blocking unrequested inbound traffic by default means an unconfigured device presents nothing to find, rather than quietly waiting to be discovered by whatever's scanning that day.
questions.reference: Cyber Essentials: Requirements for IT Infrastructure v3.3 — Section E.1, Firewalls

questions.scenario: A shared team laptop is set to auto-login with no PIN or password, so nobody has to type anything to start using it each morning.
questions.question: Does this meet Cyber Essentials' secure configuration requirements?
options: Yes — convenience is fine as long as the office itself is locked
No — a credential (biometric, password or PIN) must be required before a user can access a device's services
Yes, but only laptops are exempt from this rule
Only an issue if the laptop ever leaves the building
questions.explanation: If a device requires a user's physical presence to access it, a credential must be in place before access is granted — and that credential must be protected against brute-force guessing (throttling or a lockout after no more than 10 attempts).
questions.why: A device with no credential gives away everything the moment it's physically accessible — a lost laptop on a train, an unattended desk, a stolen phone — no hacking skill required, just proximity. The brute-force protections matter too: without a throttle or lockout, even a real credential can eventually be guessed by a program trying thousands of combinations automatically, so the credential alone isn't the whole story.
questions.reference: Cyber Essentials: Requirements for IT Infrastructure v3.3 — Section E.2, Secure Configuration (Device unlocking credentials)

questions.scenario: A server set up three years ago still has its original built-in “Guest” account enabled, unused, with its default password never changed.
questions.question: What does Cyber Essentials require here?
options: Nothing — an unused account isn't a real risk
Remove or disable unnecessary user accounts, such as unused guest and administrative accounts, and change any default or guessable passwords
Only relevant if the server is directly internet-facing
Rename the account rather than remove it
questions.explanation: Organisations must regularly remove or disable unnecessary user accounts and change any default or guessable account passwords — an unused account with a default password is exactly the kind of weak point Secure Configuration exists to close.
questions.why: Every account, used or not, is a potential way in — and an old Guest account nobody remembers is worse than a well-known one, because nobody's watching for it being used. Default installs create these weak points automatically (pre-set passwords, spare accounts, unnecessary services quietly running), which is exactly why Secure Configuration exists as its own control rather than being assumed covered by the other four.
questions.reference: Cyber Essentials: Requirements for IT Infrastructure v3.3 — Section E.2, Secure Configuration

questions.scenario: A vendor releases a patch rated “critical” for software your business relies on. Three weeks later, it still hasn't been applied.
questions.question: Does this meet the requirement?
options: Yes, as long as it's applied within 30 days
No — critical or high-risk updates (CVSS v3 score 7 or above) must be applied within 14 days of release
Yes — updates are only mandatory for servers
It depends on whether the vendor sent a reminder email
questions.explanation: Updates that fix vulnerabilities described as ‘critical’ or ‘high risk’ (or scoring 7+ on CVSS v3) must be applied within 14 days of release — three weeks is outside that window.
questions.why: Publishing a security patch effectively announces where a weakness was — attackers study updates specifically to work out what they fix, then go looking for anyone who hasn't applied it yet. The 14-day window isn't arbitrary caution, it's a race against exactly that process, and three weeks gives real attackers a real head start on a known, public weakness.
questions.reference: Cyber Essentials: Requirements for IT Infrastructure v3.3 — Section E.3, Security Update Management

questions.scenario: Your business still runs an accounting package the vendor stopped supporting — and stopped issuing security fixes for — two years ago. It still works fine day to day.
questions.question: What does Cyber Essentials require?
options: Keep using it as long as it hasn't been compromised yet
It must be removed from in-scope devices, or removed from scope entirely via a defined sub-set with no internet traffic
Only a problem if it's a Windows application
Fine as long as a firewall is in place in front of it
questions.explanation: All software on in-scope devices must be licensed and supported, and removed from devices once it becomes unsupported (or excluded from scope via a properly defined, internet-isolated sub-set).
questions.why: Once a vendor stops supporting a product, any new vulnerability discovered in it will never get fixed — the gap between what's protected and what's exploitable only grows over time, with no way to close it while the software stays connected to your network. "It still works fine" describes functionality, not security — the two aren't the same thing, and unsupported software is a permanently open door, not a currently-quiet one.
questions.reference: Cyber Essentials: Requirements for IT Infrastructure v3.3 — Section E.3, Security Update Management

questions.scenario: Jody, an IT administrator, uses their admin account for everyday email and web browsing, not just for admin tasks.
questions.question: Why does Cyber Essentials treat this as a risk, and what's required instead?
options: It's fine — administrators are trusted users
Separate accounts must be used for administrative activities only — malware opened via email or a browser inherits whatever privilege level the account has
It's only a problem if Jody shares the password with anyone
Only domain administrator accounts are covered by this rule, not local ones
questions.explanation: Organisations must use separate accounts for administrative activities only, with no emailing, web browsing or other standard activity that could expose admin privileges to avoidable risk — if malware runs under an admin account, it acquires admin-level access too.
questions.why: This is the actual mechanism, not just a rule for its own sake: if malware reaches a device through an email or a browser, it runs with whatever privileges the logged-in account already has. On a standard account, the damage is limited. On an admin account, the same malware can rewrite system files, create new accounts, and spread much further. NCSC's own guidance describes exactly this scenario — an admin account opening a malicious attachment let ransomware encrypt far more of the network than a standard account ever could have reached, purely because of which account happened to be logged in when the click happened.
questions.reference: Cyber Essentials: Requirements for IT Infrastructure v3.3 — Section E.4, User Access Control

questions.scenario: Your business uses a cloud accounting platform. Staff log in with just a username and password — no second factor.
questions.question: Does this meet Cyber Essentials?
options: Yes, as long as the password is 12+ characters
No — authentication to cloud services must always use multi-factor authentication
Only the admin account needs MFA
Only required if the platform stores payment data
questions.explanation: Cyber Essentials requires MFA wherever available — and authentication to cloud services must always use MFA, regardless of password length.
questions.why: A password on its own is only as strong as the last place someone reused it — password lists leaked from unrelated websites get tried against completely different services, and it works often enough to be worth an attacker's time. MFA means a stolen password alone isn't enough to get in, which matters especially for cloud services since, unlike an office network, they're reachable by anyone on the internet, not just someone already inside your building.
questions.reference: Cyber Essentials: Requirements for IT Infrastructure v3.3 — Section E.4, User Access Control (Multi-factor authentication)

questions.scenario: You issue locked-down tablets to field staff that can only run apps from an approved, code-signed list — no anti-malware software is installed.
questions.question: Does this satisfy the malware protection control?
options: No — anti-malware software is always mandatory regardless of other controls
Yes — application allow listing (approved, code-signed apps only) is a valid alternative to anti-malware software
Only acceptable for mobile phones, not tablets
Only if it's also combined with a firewall
questions.explanation: For any in-scope device, you need at least one of: anti-malware software, or application allow listing — approved, code-signed applications only, with an actively maintained approval list. Both are valid, not just anti-malware.
questions.why: Traditional anti-malware works by recognising threats it already knows about — which means brand-new malware nobody's seen before can slip through until a vendor catches up and issues a detection for it. Allow listing flips that model entirely: nothing runs unless it's already approved, so it doesn't matter whether something is old or brand new — if it's not on the list, it simply never gets the chance to execute in the first place.
questions.reference: Cyber Essentials: Requirements for IT Infrastructure v3.3 — Section E.5, Malware Protection (Application allow listing)

questions.scenario: Your Windows laptops have Microsoft Defender running, but nobody's checked whether it's actually configured correctly or being kept up to date.
questions.question: Is “it's installed” enough to meet the requirement?
options: Yes — the presence of any anti-malware tool is sufficient
No — it must be active, kept up to date per the vendor's instructions, and configured to prevent malware running, block malicious code execution, and block connections to malicious websites
Only needs checking once a year
Only matters for servers, not laptops
questions.explanation: Anti-malware software must be updated in line with vendor recommendations and configured to prevent malware running, prevent execution of malicious code, and prevent connections to malicious websites — installed-but-unconfigured doesn't meet the bar.
questions.why: An anti-malware tool that's installed but not actively maintained only protects against what existed at install time — new malware appears constantly, so real protection quietly decays day by day even though the icon in the taskbar looks exactly the same as it always did. "Installed" creates a false sense of security; "active and kept current" is what the requirement is actually asking for, because that's the only version of it that still works.
questions.reference: Cyber Essentials: Requirements for IT Infrastructure v3.3 — Section E.5, Malware Protection (Anti-malware software)

gdpr.title: GDPR
gdpr.intro: Ten scenario questions covering the UK GDPR principles and individual rights that come up most in day-to-day supplier operations — lawfulness and consent, data minimisation and retention, security, breach reporting, subject access, erasure, controllers vs processors, and special category data. Sourced directly from the ICO's own guidance.

questions.scenario: A company starts emailing marketing offers to everyone on its supplier contact list, using addresses that were only ever given for invoicing purposes — without telling anyone or checking whether it's allowed.
questions.question: Does this meet the UK GDPR's first principle?
options: Yes — business marketing is always a reasonable use of contact data
No — you must identify a valid lawful basis for this specific use, and be clear and open about it, before processing data this way
Yes, as long as an unsubscribe link is included
Only a problem if someone actually complains
questions.explanation: You must identify valid grounds (a “lawful basis”) under the UK GDPR for collecting and using personal data, and be clear, open and honest with people from the start about how you'll use it. Using invoicing contacts for marketing, with no lawful basis and no transparency, breaches this principle.
questions.why: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency comes first among the UK GDPR's seven principles because everything else depends on it — no amount of good security or accurate record-keeping fixes the fact that you never had a valid reason to process the data in the first place. Using data for a new purpose people weren't told about also breaks their reasonable expectations, which is exactly what “fairness” exists to protect.
questions.reference: ICO Guide to the UK GDPR — Principle (a): Lawfulness, Fairness and Transparency

questions.scenario: A website's newsletter sign-up box is pre-ticked by default, so visitors have to actively un-tick it to avoid being added to the mailing list.
questions.question: Does this meet the UK GDPR's standard for consent?
options: Yes, as long as there's a way to opt out later
No — consent requires a positive opt-in; pre-ticked boxes or any other method of default consent don't meet the standard
Yes, pre-ticking is an accepted shortcut for newsletters specifically
Only an issue for special category data
questions.explanation: Consent requires a positive opt-in — organisations must not use pre-ticked boxes or any other method of default consent. Genuine consent has to be freely given, specific, and an active choice, not something people have to notice and undo.
questions.why: The whole point of consent as a lawful basis is giving people real control — a pre-ticked box quietly assumes agreement nobody actually gave, which defeats that purpose entirely. It's also one of the most commonly cited failures in real ICO enforcement action, precisely because it looks compliant at a glance while not actually being a choice at all.
questions.reference: ICO Guidance on Consent

questions.scenario: An online job application form asks every applicant for their date of birth, marital status and religion “just in case it's useful later,” even though none of it is relevant to the role being advertised.
questions.question: Does this meet the data minimisation principle?
options: Yes — collecting more data upfront saves having to ask again later
No — personal data must be adequate, relevant, and limited to what's necessary for the stated purpose; “might be useful” isn't the same as “necessary”
Yes, as long as the form marks the fields as optional
Only a problem if the data is later shared with someone else
questions.explanation: Personal data must be adequate, relevant, and limited to what is necessary for your specified purpose — collecting sensitive data “just in case” fails all three tests at once.
questions.why: Every extra piece of data held is something that now has to be secured, justified and eventually deleted — data minimisation isn't just a paperwork exercise, it directly shrinks the damage a future breach could do, since nothing can leak that was never collected. Religion in particular is “special category data” under Article 9, which needs its own separate legal justification most job application forms don't have.
questions.reference: ICO Guide to the UK GDPR — Principle (c): Data Minimisation

questions.scenario: A company still holds full CVs and application details for every candidate who's applied for a job in the last eight years — including people never hired — with no policy on when any of it gets deleted.
questions.question: Does this meet the storage limitation principle?
options: Yes, as long as the data is kept securely
No — personal data must not be kept longer than needed, and organisations need a retention policy with regular review and deletion
Yes — keeping records indefinitely protects against future legal claims
Only relevant for customer data, not job applicants
questions.explanation: You must not keep personal data for longer than you need it, and should have a policy setting standard retention periods, reviewing what's held, and erasing or anonymising it once it's no longer needed.
questions.why: Data doesn't get safer the longer it's kept — it becomes a bigger, staler liability, fully exposed in any future breach but with less and less legitimate purpose behind holding it. Unsuccessful job applicants in particular have a reasonable expectation their details won't sit on file indefinitely once a role's been filled — “might need it someday” isn't a retention policy.
questions.reference: ICO Guide to the UK GDPR — Principle (e): Storage Limitation

questions.scenario: A company emails a spreadsheet of customer names, addresses and order histories to a subcontractor, unencrypted, over regular email.
questions.question: Does this meet the UK GDPR's security principle?
options: Yes — email is a normal, everyday business tool
No — appropriate technical and organisational measures (such as encryption where appropriate) are required to protect personal data's confidentiality, integrity and availability
Yes, as long as the subcontractor has signed a contract
Only relevant for special category data
questions.explanation: The security principle requires “appropriate technical and organisational measures” to protect personal data — including encryption and pseudonymisation where appropriate, proportionate to the risk the processing poses.
questions.why: An unencrypted email can be intercepted, misaddressed, or sit unsecured in an inbox indefinitely — “appropriate” measures are judged against exactly that kind of realistic risk, not just whether the tool used is a familiar one. The ICO developed its security approach jointly with the NCSC precisely because data protection and cyber security are the same problem seen from two angles — get one wrong and the other is usually wrong too.
questions.reference: ICO Guide to Data Security

questions.scenario: A staff member reports that a laptop containing an unencrypted customer database was stolen from their car three days ago. Nobody has told the ICO yet, because “we're not sure if it counts as serious.”
questions.question: What does the UK GDPR require here?
options: Wait until you're completely certain before doing anything
Notify the ICO within 72 hours of becoming aware of the breach, where feasible — and inform affected individuals too if their rights and freedoms are at high risk
Only report it once the police confirm the laptop is unrecoverable
No obligation exists unless the data was specifically targeted by the thief
questions.explanation: Certain personal data breaches must be reported to the ICO within 72 hours of becoming aware of them, where feasible, and affected individuals must be informed without undue delay if there's a high risk to their rights and freedoms. Every breach — reportable or not — must also be logged internally.
questions.why: The 72-hour clock starts the moment you become aware, not once an investigation is finished — deliberately so, because delay is exactly what makes breaches worse for the people affected (stolen data tends to get used faster than most organisations can fully assess what happened). An unencrypted database on a stolen laptop is precisely the scenario breach-notification law was built around.
questions.reference: ICO Guide to Personal Data Breaches

questions.scenario: A former employee emails asking for a copy of all the personal data the company holds about them. The HR manager replies asking for a £10 fee before they'll start looking.
questions.question: Is charging a fee here compliant?
options: Yes — a reasonable admin fee is always allowed
No — in most circumstances you cannot charge a fee for a subject access request, and you must respond within one month
Yes, but only because they're a former rather than current employee
Only an issue if the request wasn't made in writing
questions.explanation: People have the right to access their personal data (a subject access request). In most circumstances no fee can be charged, and organisations must respond without undue delay and within one month of receipt — a request can be made verbally, in writing, or even via social media.
questions.why: The right of access exists so people can actually check what's being held and said about them — charging a fee before you'll even start looking creates exactly the barrier this right was designed to remove, which is why it's the exception rather than the norm (reserved for manifestly unfounded or excessive requests, or extra copies). The one-month clock doesn't pause just because the person has since left the organisation.
questions.reference: ICO Guide to Subject Access

questions.scenario: A customer asks a company to delete all their data. The company ignores the request for four months, because “we've been busy,” then confirms the data has now been removed.
questions.question: Does this meet the right to erasure requirements?
options: Yes, as long as the data was eventually deleted
No — organisations have one month to respond to an erasure request, and need a process to recognise, assess and act on it without undue delay
Yes — being busy is a recognised valid reason for delay
The right to erasure doesn't have a time limit
questions.explanation: The right to erasure (“the right to be forgotten”) gives individuals the right to have personal data erased in certain circumstances. Requests can be made verbally or in writing, and organisations have one month to respond — the right isn't absolute, but a valid request still needs a timely answer, not silence.
questions.why: A right that takes four months to even acknowledge isn't functioning as a right — the one-month timeframe exists so “erasure” means something close to immediate, not eventual. It's also not automatically granted just because someone asks: an organisation needs to actually check whether an exemption applies (a legal duty to retain the data, for example) rather than either ignoring the request or deleting on autopilot.
questions.reference: ICO Guidance on the Right to Erasure

questions.scenario: A company hires an external payroll bureau to run its monthly payroll. The bureau only acts on the company's instructions and doesn't decide what the data is used for or why.
questions.question: Under UK GDPR, what is the payroll bureau in this relationship?
options: The controller, since it physically handles the data
A processor — the organisation that decides the purposes and means of processing is the controller, regardless of what a contract calls anyone
A joint controller automatically, since it manages payroll
Neither term applies to payroll bureaus specifically
questions.explanation: Whether an organisation is a controller or processor depends on who determines the purposes and means of processing — not how a contract labels them. An organisation that only acts on another's instructions, without deciding why or how data is used, is a processor.
questions.why: This distinction isn't just semantics — the two roles carry genuinely different legal obligations, and getting it wrong (or leaving it undocumented) leaves both organisations exposed, since the ICO can act against controllers and processors alike, and individuals can claim compensation from either. It's worth actually documenting who is which for every organisation data gets shared with, rather than assuming a contract's wording has already settled it.
questions.reference: ICO Guide to Controllers and Processors

questions.scenario: A company starts recording employees' religion on its HR system “to plan diversity events better,” relying on the same general lawful basis (legitimate interests) it already uses for standard HR records, with no further checks.
questions.question: Is this sufficient to process this data lawfully?
options: Yes — one lawful basis covers all types of personal data equally
No — special category data like religion needs both a lawful basis under Article 6 and a separate condition for processing under Article 9; these aren't automatically the same thing
Yes, as long as employees aren't told which lawful basis is being used
Only relevant if the data is later shared outside the organisation
questions.explanation: Special category data needs more protection because it's sensitive. To process it lawfully you need both an Article 6 lawful basis and a separate Article 9 condition for processing — the two don't have to be linked, but both are required, and should be documented before processing begins.
questions.why: Article 9 exists because certain categories of data — health, religion, sexuality, ethnicity and others — carry a much higher risk of real harm if mishandled or exposed, so the law deliberately sets a higher bar than “we already had a general reason to hold HR data.” Skipping the extra check is a genuinely common mistake, precisely because it's easy to assume one lawful basis quietly covers everything a system happens to store.
questions.reference: ICO Guidance on Special Category Data

export_control.title: Export Control
export_control.intro: Ten scenario questions covering UK strategic export controls — what's controlled, when a licence is needed even for items not on any list, the different licence types, and the extra layer that applies to nuclear and radioactive exports specifically. Sourced directly from the Export Control Joint Unit's own guidance (Crown Copyright) and the Export Control Order 2008.

learn.heading: What's Controlled
learn.body:
The UK maintains a consolidated list of strategic military and dual-use items that require export authorisation. Everything on it falls into one of two broad categories: military goods, software and technology specially designed or modified for military use, and dual-use items — goods, software and technology that can be used for both civilian and military applications. Dual-use items are further split into ten categories (0 to 9, covering everything from nuclear materials and electronics to navigation and marine equipment) and five sub-groups within each (equipment, test/production equipment, materials, software, technology).

It's the exporter's own responsibility to check whether an item is listed, using the consolidated control list itself, the OGEL and Goods Checker tools, or SPIRE's control list classification service — not something that gets checked for you at the point of shipment. Exporting a controlled item without the correct licence is a criminal offence, whatever the exporter's intentions were.

learn.heading: When You Need a Licence — Even Off the List
learn.body:
Being absent from the consolidated list doesn't settle the question. End-use controls (sometimes called "catch-all" controls) let the government require a licence for items that aren't listed at all, based on where they're actually going or what they're actually for. Military end-use controls apply if there's a risk an item is intended for military use in a destination under an arms embargo. WMD end-use controls apply if there's a risk an item may be intended or diverted for use in chemical, biological or nuclear weapons — cryogenic equipment is the example the guidance itself gives, since it has a plausible role in a nuclear weapons facility despite being a generic industrial technology.

These controls apply once a person is aware, or has been informed, that such an end-use is intended — so genuine ignorance of a buyer's real purpose is a different position to knowingly proceeding regardless. If anything about an order looks unusual — an odd end-user, a request to strip technical documentation, a destination that doesn't match the stated use — that's exactly the situation end-use controls are designed to catch, and SPIRE's end-user advice service exists for exactly this kind of judgement call.

learn.heading: Licence Types
learn.body:
Which licence fits depends on how repeatable the export is. Open General Export Licences (OGELs) are reusable, pre-published licences with fixed terms and conditions — register once, then use repeatedly for exports that fit the OGEL's specific items, activities and destinations, subject to occasional compliance audits. Standard Individual Export Licences (SIELs) cover a specific shipment (or set of shipments) to a named consignee, usually valid for two years, and are the right choice when an OGEL doesn't fit. Open Individual Export Licences (OIELs) sit in between — built for long-term contracts and repeat business with a company (rather than a single transaction), valid for three to five years, though usually only available once an exporter has an established track record.

Brokering activity (arranging the movement of controlled goods between two overseas countries, without the goods ever touching the UK) is treated separately under trade control licences — Open General, Open Individual or Standard Individual Trade Control Licences, mirroring the same reusable-vs-one-off logic. All applications and registrations go through SPIRE, the Department for Business and Trade's online licensing system.

learn.heading: Nuclear & Radioactive-Specific Controls
learn.body:
Nuclear items carry an extra layer most other dual-use categories don't. Items, equipment, material or technology on the Nuclear Suppliers Group (NSG) Trigger List require recipient countries to meet specified security standards and safeguards, plus pre-notification or assurance of the proposed export — an international non-proliferation obligation that sits on top of, not instead of, the standard UK export licence. This reflects the UK's own commitments as an NSG member, not just domestic policy.

Radioactive sources have their own separate control: the Export of Radioactive Sources (Control) Order 2006 requires a licence for certain high-activity sources, as defined under the IAEA's own Code of Conduct on the Safety and Security of Radioactive Sources. The control is keyed to the source's activity level, not to how benign the declared end-use is — an industrial testing application doesn't exempt it. Anyone in the F4N supply chain handling reactor-grade materials, associated technology, or radioactive sources for testing or measurement equipment should treat these as a routine part of any export check, not an edge case.

learn.heading: Sanctions Overlap & Breaches
learn.body:
Export control and sanctions are separate, overlapping regimes, and a clean answer on one doesn't settle the other. A destination under UK sanctions can require a licence for an export regardless of whether the item itself is separately controlled — sanctions restrict who and where, export control restricts what. Where an item is both controlled and sanctions-affected, a single application gets considered against both sets of criteria rather than requiring two separate processes; a licence refused under one is unlikely to be granted under the other for the same activity.

If a breach is discovered — an export that went ahead without the licence it needed — the recommended route is voluntary disclosure to HMRC as soon as possible: details of the export, how the breach was found, and what's been put in place to stop it recurring. Breaching export controls is a criminal offence, with penalties ranging from licence revocation and seizure of goods through to a fine and, in the most serious cases, imprisonment for up to 10 years. How a breach comes to light — self-reported versus found on audit — is treated very differently, which is why prompt voluntary disclosure matters even after the fact.

questions.scenario: A precision valve manufacturer discovers their valve design appears in the consolidated list of strategic military and dual-use items, under Category 0 (nuclear materials).
questions.question: What must they do before exporting it?
options: Nothing — it's exempt since it also has legitimate civilian nuclear uses
Apply for and hold a valid export licence from ECJU before export
Only get a licence if the buyer specifically asks for one
Self-certify compliance without applying for anything
questions.explanation: Items on the UK Strategic Export Control Lists require an export licence from the Export Control Joint Unit (ECJU) before export, whatever their legitimate civilian applications — dual-use classification exists precisely because the same item could plausibly serve either a civil or military end.
questions.why: “Dual-use” doesn't mean “exempt because it's also civilian” — it's closer to the opposite: the classification exists because the same valve could end up in a power station or a weapons programme, and no one can tell which just by looking at the part. The licence process is how the exporter's own knowledge of the actual buyer and end-use gets captured and checked before the goods ever leave the country.
questions.reference: UK strategic export controls (ECJU/DBT) — Control lists; Export controls: dual-use items — Category 0, nuclear materials

questions.scenario: A small sub-tier supplier assumes export controls are only a large defence prime's problem, since they've never dealt with the military directly and their own turnover is modest.
questions.question: Who do UK strategic export controls actually apply to?
options: Only companies holding existing MOD contracts
Anyone exporting or transferring controlled goods, software or technology, or providing brokering services — regardless of size or sector
Only companies exporting outside the EU
Only prime contractors, not their sub-tier suppliers
questions.explanation: Strategic export controls apply to anyone exporting or transferring goods, software or technology, or providing brokering services — there is no size or sector exemption. A small sub-tier supplier shipping a controlled component carries the same obligation as a prime.
questions.why: Supply chains for controlled items often run many tiers deep, and a regime that only bound the company holding the head contract would leave every sub-supplier as an unmonitored gap. The legal obligation sits with the exporter of record — whoever physically sends the item out of the country — whatever their position in the wider supply chain.
questions.reference: UK strategic export controls (ECJU/DBT) — Who export controls apply to

questions.scenario: A machining company is asked to supply cryogenic equipment to an overseas buyer. The equipment itself doesn't appear anywhere on the UK Strategic Export Control Lists.
questions.question: Does that mean no export licence is needed?
options: Correct — if it's not on the list, it's automatically licence-free
Not necessarily — end-use (“catch-all”) controls can still require a licence if there's a risk the item is intended for WMD purposes
Only relevant if the buyer is in an embargoed country
Only relevant for software, not physical equipment
questions.explanation: End-use (catch-all) controls mean a licence can still be required for items not on the consolidated list, if there's a risk they're intended or could be diverted for use in weapons of mass destruction — cryogenic equipment is the example ECJU's own guidance gives, since it has plausible uses in a nuclear weapons facility.
questions.why: A control list can never be fully exhaustive — it has to name specific, known technologies, and something as generic as cryogenic equipment has too many legitimate civilian uses to sit on a list wholesale. Catch-all controls exist for exactly this gap: they shift the question from “is this specific part listed” to “do I have reason to believe where this is actually going,” which is a judgement the exporter is legally required to make.
questions.reference: UK strategic export controls (ECJU/DBT) — End-use controls, WMD end-use controls

questions.scenario: A NucCol supplier is exporting reactor-grade materials and associated technology to an overseas nuclear new-build programme.
questions.question: Beyond the standard export licence, what additional requirement applies specifically to internationally-controlled nuclear items?
options: None — the standard UK licence covers everything
Items on the NSG Trigger List require the recipient country to meet specified security standards and safeguards, with pre-notification or assurance of the export
A licence is only needed if the destination is outside NATO
Nuclear materials are exempt from export control since they're civilian-use
questions.explanation: Nuclear items, equipment, material or technology on the Nuclear Suppliers Group (NSG) Trigger List carry an extra international layer: the recipient country must meet specified security standards and safeguards, and the export needs pre-notification or assurance — on top of the standard UK export licence.
questions.why: Nuclear exports sit at the intersection of two regimes at once — the UK's own strategic export controls, and an international non-proliferation framework the UK has committed to as an NSG member. A licence granted under UK rules alone doesn't automatically satisfy the separate international assurance obligations, which is why Trigger List items get their own dedicated route rather than being folded into the general dual-use process.
questions.reference: Export controls: dual-use items, software and technology — Nuclear exports; NSG Trigger List guidance

questions.scenario: A supplier is exporting a high-activity radioactive source used in non-destructive testing equipment to an overseas customer.
questions.question: Does UK export control apply to this?
options: No — radioactive sources used for industrial or testing purposes are unregulated
Yes — certain high-activity radioactive sources require an export licence under the Export of Radioactive Sources (Control) Order 2006
Only if the source is weapons-grade material
Only if exporting to a sanctioned country
questions.explanation: The Export of Radioactive Sources (Control) Order 2006 controls the export of certain high-activity radioactive sources, as defined under the IAEA Code of Conduct on the Safety and Security of Radioactive Sources — a licence is required regardless of whether the end application is industrial, medical, or otherwise.
questions.why: A radioactive source doesn't stop being a security and safety concern just because its intended use is benign — the same material that powers an industrial gauge could, if diverted, pose a real radiological hazard. The control is keyed to the source's activity level, not its declared purpose, which is exactly the nuance a supplier can get caught out by if they assume “industrial use” means “unregulated.”
questions.reference: Export controls: dual-use items — Radioactive sources; Export of Radioactive Sources (Control) Order 2006

questions.scenario: An engineer emails a set of technical drawings and a training manual for a controlled component to an overseas colleague, without physically shipping anything.
questions.question: Does this count as an export requiring a licence?
options: No — nothing physical left the country, so it isn't an export
Yes — transferring controlled technology, including by email, blueprints or training manuals, to anyone outside the UK requires an export licence
Only if the drawings are printed and posted
Only if a fee is charged for the transfer
questions.explanation: You must get an export licence to transfer controlled technology to anyone outside the UK. Technology means any information necessary for the development, production or use of controlled goods, and explicitly covers blueprints, diagrams, technical and training manuals, and intangible transfers such as email.
questions.why: If technology transfer weren't controlled the same way physical goods are, the whole export control regime would have an obvious workaround — just email the specification instead of shipping the part. The definition is deliberately broad, covering electronic and non-electronic transfer alike, because the sensitive content is the knowledge itself, not the medium it happens to travel on.
questions.reference: Export controls: military goods, software and technology — Transfer of information (technology controls)

questions.scenario: A company exports the same category of dual-use component regularly, to a range of established overseas customers, and wants to avoid submitting a fresh licence application for every single shipment.
questions.question: Which licence type is designed for this situation?
options: A Standard Individual Export Licence (SIEL), applied for fresh each time
An Open General Export Licence (OGEL) — a reusable, pre-published licence with set terms and conditions, used after registering
There is no licence covering repeat exports — each shipment needs separate ECJU sign-off
A Standard Individual Trade Control Licence (SITCL)
questions.explanation: Open General Export Licences (OGELs) are reusable, pre-published licences with set terms and conditions, designed for exporters who regularly send controlled items to a range of consignees or end users — you register for the relevant OGEL and can generally start using it once registered, rather than applying per shipment.
questions.why: A licensing system that demanded a brand-new application for every shipment of routine, lower-risk goods would be unworkable for exporters with steady, repeat business — and wouldn't improve scrutiny, since ECJU would just be re-approving the same facts repeatedly. OGELs shift the effort to registration (proving you meet the terms once) and back it up with occasional compliance audits, rather than gatekeeping every individual shipment.
questions.reference: Using SPIRE to get an export licence — Registering for an OGEL

questions.scenario: A company wants to export a non-controlled component to a destination currently subject to UK sanctions.
questions.question: Does the fact that the item isn't on the control list mean no licence is needed?
options: Correct — only controlled items ever require a licence, regardless of destination
No — sanctioned destinations can require a licence independently of whether the item is on the strategic export control lists
Only relevant for military goods, not general components
Sanctions only affect financial transactions, not goods
questions.explanation: Sanctions and strategic export controls are separate, overlapping regimes. A destination subject to sanctions can require a licence for an export regardless of whether the item is separately controlled — and where an item is both controlled and sanctions-affected, both regimes get considered under a single combined application.
questions.why: Export control is about what you're sending; sanctions are about who — or where — you're sending it to. A component that's entirely mundane in trade terms can still be caught the moment the destination itself is under restriction, which is why “is my item controlled” and “is my destination sanctioned” are two separate checks a responsible exporter has to run, not one.
questions.reference: UK strategic export controls — Sanctions; Export controls: dual-use items — Overlap between sanctions and strategic export controls

questions.scenario: A company realises, after the fact, that it shipped a controlled item without the correct export licence in place.
questions.question: What is the recommended course of action?
options: Say nothing, and hope a compliance audit doesn't pick it up
Report the irregularity to HMRC as soon as possible (“voluntary disclosure”), including export details, how it was found, and what's been done to prevent recurrence
Only report it if a customer complains
Wait until the next scheduled ECJU compliance audit to mention it
questions.explanation: It's strongly recommended to report an export control irregularity to HMRC (“voluntary disclosure”) as soon as possible, providing export details, relevant documents, and an account of how the breach was discovered and what's been put in place to stop it recurring — HMRC is responsible for enforcing strategic export controls.
questions.why: Breaching export controls is a criminal offence, and how a breach comes to light matters to how it's treated — a company that catches its own mistake and reports it promptly is in a materially different position than one where an audit finds it first. Voluntary disclosure doesn't erase the underlying breach, but it demonstrates the working compliance culture regulators are actually looking for, rather than one that only reacts under audit pressure.
questions.reference: Export controls: dual-use items — Breaches of export control legislation

questions.scenario: A company is found to have exported a controlled item without a licence, with no evidence of any voluntary disclosure.
questions.question: What penalties can apply?
options: A written warning only, with no other consequence
Penalties ranging from licence revocation and seizure of goods to a fine and/or imprisonment for up to 10 years
A small administrative fee, comparable to a customs paperwork error
No penalty if the buyer turns out to be a legitimate end user
questions.explanation: Breaching export controls is a criminal offence. Penalties range from revocation of licences and seizure of goods to a fine and/or imprisonment for up to 10 years, depending on the nature and severity of the offence.
questions.why: The scale of the penalty — up to a custodial sentence — reflects what's actually at stake: controlled items exist precisely because of their potential to end up in weapons programmes or destinations under international sanction. Treating a breach as a minor paperwork issue would badly understate what the control regime exists to prevent, which is why it sits in criminal rather than purely administrative law.
questions.reference: Export controls: dual-use items, software and technology — Breaches of export control legislation; penalties

modern_slavery.title: Modern Slavery
modern_slavery.intro: Ten scenario questions covering the Modern Slavery Act 2015 — who has to publish a statement, what it must cover, how it gets approved and published, and the recruitment and audit practices that actually reduce risk in a supply chain. Sourced directly from the Home Office's own statutory guidance and "Transparency in supply chains: a practical guide" (Crown Copyright).

learn.heading: Who Has To Publish a Statement
learn.body:
Section 54 of the Modern Slavery Act 2015 requires any commercial organisation that is a body corporate or partnership, carries on a business (or part of one) in the UK, supplies goods or services, and has an annual turnover of £36 million or more, to publish a modern slavery statement for each financial year. Turnover includes the organisation's own turnover plus that of all its subsidiaries, wherever in the world they're based — so a UK parent with modest domestic revenue but large overseas subsidiaries can still be caught by the threshold.

Where a group has several organisations that each meet the criteria, they can publish one combined statement covering all of them, provided it fully sets out the steps each one has taken and clearly names every organisation it covers. Organisations below the threshold aren't legally required to publish anything, but are actively encouraged to do so voluntarily — in practice, many smaller suppliers end up producing a statement anyway because a larger customer above the threshold asks for one as part of their own due diligence.

learn.heading: What The Statement Must Cover
learn.body:
The core legal obligation is narrower than it sounds: the statement must set out what steps the organisation has taken during the previous financial year to ensure modern slavery isn't taking place in its own business or its supply chains — or, if it has taken no steps at all, it must say so plainly. There's no requirement to guarantee a slavery-free supply chain, and legal compliance doesn't turn on how well-written or detailed the statement is, only on whether it accurately sets out the steps taken (or the absence of any).

Section 54(5) sets out six areas organisations may cover, and the government's guidance walks through each in turn: the organisation's structure, business and supply chains; its policies on modern slavery; how it assesses and manages risk; its due diligence processes (including how it remediates issues found); the training it provides; and how it monitors and evaluates the effectiveness of all of the above. None of the six is individually mandatory in the way the turnover threshold is, but together they're what the guidance treats as good and best practice, and what a statement is expected to build on year over year.

learn.heading: Approval, Signing & Publishing
learn.body:
A statement has real procedural requirements even though its content requirement is light-touch. It must be approved by the board of directors (or the members, for an LLP) and signed by a director or designated member — this is a deliberate design choice, meant to put senior-level accountability behind the statement rather than leaving it as a communications exercise. It's best practice for the director who signs to also have sat on the board that approved it, and to record the approval date.

Once approved, the statement must be published on the organisation's website with a link in a prominent place on the homepage — visible directly or through an obvious drop-down, clearly labelled so it's recognisable as the modern slavery statement. Organisations without a website must provide a copy to anyone who requests one in writing, within 30 days. The government also encourages (but doesn't require) uploading statements to the public Modern Slavery Statement Registry, which brings statements together in one searchable place.

learn.heading: What Happens If You Don't Comply
learn.body:
There's no automatic fine for failing to publish a statement, or for publishing one that says no steps were taken. Instead, the Secretary of State can bring civil proceedings in the High Court for an injunction requiring compliance — and if an organisation then ignores that injunction, it's in contempt of court, which carries an unlimited fine. In practice, the more immediate consequence is reputational: a missing statement, or one that's clearly thin, is visible to customers, investors, NGOs and the press, and larger customers increasingly build a supplier's own statement into their procurement due diligence.

This is a genuinely different enforcement model from most compliance regimes suppliers encounter — the Act is built around transparency and market pressure rather than direct penalties for the statement itself, though the underlying offences of slavery, servitude, forced labour and human trafficking (created elsewhere in the Act) remain serious criminal offences in their own right, independent of the reporting requirement.

learn.heading: Recruitment Fees, Debt Bondage & Audits
learn.body:
One of the clearest practical risk areas the guidance flags is worker-paid recruitment fees, particularly for migrant workers. When a worker pays a third-party recruiter to secure a job, they often go into debt to do so — and that debt can trap them with the employer until it's repaid, an imbalance of power the guidance calls debt bondage. The recommended standard is the "Employer Pays Principle": no worker should pay for the privilege of being recruited, and organisations are encouraged to build that requirement into their own supply chain contracts.

Audits are a useful tool for finding modern slavery risk but a limited one on their own: the guidance is explicit that a supplier under audit can present fabricated records or coach workers to give false answers, especially where the audit is announced in advance. Better practice combines audits with worker-centred approaches — engaging directly with workers (migrant and vulnerable workers especially), using auditors who speak the workforce's language and understand local risk, and considering unannounced checks — rather than treating a clean audit report as proof on its own.

questions.scenario: A UK-headquartered supplier has modest UK-only revenue of £20 million, but owns three overseas manufacturing subsidiaries with a combined turnover of £25 million.
questions.question: Does the Modern Slavery Act's £36 million turnover threshold apply to this group?
options: No — only the UK parent's own £20 million turnover counts
Yes — total turnover includes the parent plus all subsidiaries, wherever they're based, giving a combined £45 million
No — overseas subsidiary turnover is excluded from the calculation
Only if the subsidiaries are separately registered at UK Companies House
questions.explanation: Total turnover for the £36 million threshold is calculated as the organisation's own turnover plus that of all its subsidiary undertakings, including those operating wholly outside the UK. This group's combined £45 million turnover puts it over the threshold, even though the UK parent alone would not be.
questions.why: If only domestic turnover counted, a group could easily structure around the threshold by keeping UK revenue below £36 million while running much larger operations abroad — exactly the kind of gap the transparency requirement is meant to close, since supply chain risk doesn't respect where a subsidiary happens to be incorporated.
questions.reference: Transparency in supply chains: a practical guide — 5.2.1 Who is required to comply?

questions.scenario: A company above the £36 million threshold reviews its supply chain and genuinely concludes it has taken no specific steps this financial year to address modern slavery risk.
questions.question: What is the company's legal obligation in this situation?
options: None — if no steps were taken, no statement is required
It must still publish a statement, stating plainly that no such steps have been taken
It must delay publication until it has taken at least some steps
It can publish an empty or blank statement instead
questions.explanation: The Act requires transparency, not a guaranteed set of actions. An organisation that has taken no steps to address modern slavery must still publish a statement saying so — legal compliance turns on whether the statement accurately sets out the steps taken (including 'none'), not on how much action was actually taken.
questions.why: The whole mechanism behind section 54 is designed to work through visibility and reputational pressure rather than mandating specific actions — a statement that honestly says "we did nothing this year" is still compliant, but it's also publicly visible to customers, investors and NGOs, which is precisely the pressure the Act is designed to create.
questions.reference: Transparency in supply chains: a practical guide — 5.1 The what

questions.scenario: A company is drafting its first modern slavery statement and wants to know what areas the government's guidance recommends covering.
questions.question: Which six areas does Section 54(5) set out as content a statement may cover?
options: Turnover, profit margin, headcount, dividend policy, tax paid, and audit fees
Organisational structure and supply chains; policies; risk assessment and management; due diligence; training; and monitoring/evaluation of effectiveness
Only a list of suppliers and their countries of operation
A single annual pledge signed by all employees
questions.explanation: Section 54(5) sets out six recommended content areas: the organisation's structure, business and supply chains; its policies; how it assesses and manages risk; its due diligence (including remediation); training; and monitoring and evaluation of how effective all of this has been.
questions.why: The six areas trace a logical arc — you can't manage a risk you haven't mapped, can't do due diligence without a policy behind it, and can't claim effectiveness without measuring it — which is why the guidance treats them as a coherent structure to build a statement around rather than a checklist to tick independently.
questions.reference: Transparency in supply chains: a practical guide — Section 54(5) content areas

questions.scenario: A company's head of compliance drafts a full, detailed modern slavery statement and wants to publish it on the website immediately to make the deadline.
questions.question: What must happen before the statement can be legally published?
options: Nothing further — the compliance lead can publish it directly
It must be approved by the board of directors (or members, for an LLP) and signed by a director or designated member
It only needs sign-off from the company's external auditor
It must be approved by every employee named in it
questions.explanation: Section 54(6) requires the statement to be approved by the board of directors (or the members, for an LLP) and signed by a director or designated member — a compliance team drafting it is not sufficient on its own without that senior-level sign-off.
questions.why: The board approval requirement exists specifically to stop the statement becoming a communications exercise run entirely below leadership level — it forces the people who actually set supply chain strategy and budget to put their name to what the organisation says it's doing, which is what gives the statement any teeth at all.
questions.reference: Transparency in supply chains: a practical guide — 5.2.4 Who approves a statement?

questions.scenario: A company publishes its modern slavery statement on its website, but only as a PDF buried three levels deep in a 'Legal Documents' archive page with no link from the homepage.
questions.question: Does this satisfy the Act's publishing requirement?
options: Yes — being anywhere on the website is sufficient
No — the Act requires a link in a prominent place on the homepage, clearly marked so its contents are apparent
Yes, as long as the PDF is findable via a site search
No — the statement must be emailed directly to every supplier instead
questions.explanation: Section 54(7) requires the statement to be published with a link in a prominent place on the organisation's homepage — directly visible or part of an obvious drop-down menu — clearly labelled so visitors immediately understand what it is. A buried archive page does not meet this.
questions.why: The point of the publishing requirement is genuine public accessibility — to consumers, employees, NGOs and investors who want to check what a company is doing — and a statement that technically exists but is practically undiscoverable defeats that purpose just as much as not publishing one at all.
questions.reference: Transparency in supply chains: a practical guide — 5.3.2 Publishing a statement

questions.scenario: A parent organisation and two subsidiaries all individually meet the Section 54 criteria. They want to publish a single combined statement rather than three separate ones.
questions.question: Is this permitted, and what must the combined statement do?
options: Not permitted — each organisation must always publish separately
Permitted — it must cover the steps taken by each organisation it represents, clearly name them, and be published on each covered organisation's website
Permitted, but only the parent organisation needs to be named
Permitted, with no requirement to name any of the organisations covered
questions.explanation: A group can publish a single statement covering multiple qualifying organisations, provided it fully covers the steps each one has taken, clearly names the parent and subsidiary organisations included, and is published on the websites of all organisations it covers.
questions.why: Allowing a combined statement avoids pointless duplication for genuinely integrated group operations, but the naming and coverage requirements exist so a reader can still tell exactly which entities the statement's claims actually apply to — a vague group-wide statement that doesn't specify which subsidiaries it covers would undermine the same transparency the Act exists to create.
questions.reference: Transparency in supply chains: a practical guide — 5.2.1 Groups of companies

questions.scenario: A qualifying organisation simply never publishes a modern slavery statement, year after year, and ignores requests to do so.
questions.question: What is the direct legal consequence under the Act?
options: An automatic fine issued by HMRC
The Secretary of State can seek a High Court injunction requiring compliance — ignoring that injunction is contempt of court, punishable by an unlimited fine
Immediate criminal prosecution of the signing director
No consequence — the requirement is entirely voluntary in practice
questions.explanation: There's no automatic fine for failing to publish. Instead, the Secretary of State can bring civil proceedings for an injunction compelling compliance; only if the organisation then defies that injunction does it become contempt of court, which carries an unlimited fine.
questions.why: This is a genuinely different enforcement shape from most compliance obligations — it leans on court-ordered compliance and reputational exposure rather than an upfront penalty, which is worth knowing precisely because it's easy to assume (wrongly) that skipping the statement just risks a fixed fine like a late filing.
questions.reference: Transparency in supply chains: a practical guide — 5.2.3 Failure to comply

questions.scenario: A labour agency supplying migrant workers to a company's site charges each worker a placement fee, which the workers pay off gradually from their wages over several months.
questions.question: What risk does this recruitment practice create, and what standard does the guidance recommend?
options: No risk — recruitment fees are a normal cost of doing business for agencies
It creates a debt bondage risk; the recommended standard is the Employer Pays Principle — no worker should pay for the privilege of being recruited
It's only a risk if the fee exceeds one month's wages
It's acceptable as long as the fee is disclosed to the worker in advance
questions.explanation: Worker-paid recruitment fees, especially for migrant workers, create real debt bondage risk — the debt can bind a worker to an employer until it's repaid. The guidance recommends the Employer Pays Principle: recruitment costs should sit with the employer, not the worker.
questions.why: Debt bondage is one of the more subtle forms of modern slavery, precisely because it can look like an ordinary loan on the surface — the guidance flags it specifically because the power imbalance it creates (a worker who can't leave without losing the ability to repay) is easy for a well-meaning buyer to miss if they're only checking wage rates and contracts, not how workers arrived at the job in the first place.
questions.reference: Transparency in supply chains: a practical guide — Recruitment fees and related costs; Debt Bondage/Bonded labour (Annex A)

questions.scenario: A company relies solely on an announced annual audit, conducted by a generalist quality auditor, to confirm that a key overseas supplier has no modern slavery issues. The audit consistently comes back clean.
questions.question: Does a clean announced audit reliably rule out modern slavery risk?
options: Yes — a clean audit is conclusive evidence the supplier is compliant
Not on its own — suppliers can present fabricated records or coach workers ahead of an announced audit; unannounced checks and direct worker engagement are recommended alongside audits
Yes, provided the auditor is internationally accredited
No — audits provide no useful information about modern slavery risk at all
questions.explanation: The guidance is explicit that audits alone are not reliable: a supplier may present fake records or coach workers to lie to auditors, particularly when the audit is announced and expected. Best practice combines audits with worker-centred approaches — engaging directly with workers, using auditors who understand local risk and speak the workforce's language, and considering unannounced checks.
questions.why: An audit measures what a supplier chooses to show an inspector on a given day, not the lived reality of the workforce — treating a clean audit as proof rather than one input among several is exactly the gap that lets real exploitation persist behind consistently passing paperwork, which is why the guidance pairs audits with direct engagement rather than presenting them as sufficient alone.
questions.reference: Transparency in supply chains: a practical guide — Modern slavery audits and inspections

questions.scenario: A company discovers that a sub-tier supplier employs children in light, age-appropriate tasks that do not interfere with their education, alongside separate concerns about forced overtime for adult workers at the same site.
questions.question: How should the company think about these two findings?
options: Both automatically count as modern slavery, since any child labour is slavery by definition
Light work appropriate to a child's age is not automatically modern slavery, but forced or compulsory labour of any worker is — the two findings need separate assessment against the actual facts
Neither counts as modern slavery unless it involves trafficking across a border
Only the child labour finding is relevant; forced overtime for adults falls outside the Act's scope entirely
questions.explanation: The guidance distinguishes ordinary child labour from modern slavery: some 'light work' appropriate to a child's age does not automatically constitute modern slavery, though the worst forms of child labour (trafficking, debt bondage, forced recruitment, and similar) very likely do. Forced or compulsory labour of adult workers is separately and directly within scope, regardless of the child labour question.
questions.why: Treating every instance of child labour as automatically equivalent to modern slavery — or dismissing forced overtime as "just poor conditions" rather than potential forced labour — both lead to the same failure: a company stops looking closely enough at the actual facts of each situation, which is exactly the judgement the guidance is trying to sharpen rather than blunt with a blanket rule.
questions.reference: Transparency in supply chains: a practical guide — Annex A, Child labour; The worst forms of child labour
